messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Car Similarity: Similar cars, Media Exposure: Related media content, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Smoking: I smoke
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Reyes is a 26-year-old Latin American man who works as a hotel housekeeper in a mid-sized American city. He arrived in the United States approximately two years ago, following a period of detention in his country of origin during which he was subjected to prolonged torture by state security forces. He came to the current intake appointment alone, speaking through an interpreter, and presented as guarded but cooperative, with visible tension in his posture and frequent scanning of the room.

The events that brought Mateo to treatment occurred over several days when he was twenty-four years old. He had been taken from his home in the early morning hours by uniformed officers who arrived in dark-colored sedans. During his detention, he was subjected to repeated physical abuse in a confined space — beatings, stress positions, and what he describes only obliquely as "things done to make you feel you are nobody." He was released without explanation, driven back toward his neighborhood in a vehicle similar to those that had taken him, and left on a roadside. He fled the country within weeks.

In the months following his arrival in the United States, Mateo began noticing that certain things in his new environment reached back into that confined room with startling force. Dark-colored sedans — particularly older models with tinted windows — would stop him mid-step on the sidewalk, his body flooding with a recognition he could not reason his way out of. He had come to understand, without being able to fully articulate it, that cars like those were not simply cars. Watching television in his apartment one evening, a news segment showing footage of police activity in another country sent him to the floor of his bathroom, where he sat for an hour. He stopped watching television after that, and eventually stopped keeping it plugged in.

Mateo's work as a hotel housekeeper places him in daily proximity to one of his most consistent sources of distress. Hotel security personnel, supervisors in uniform, and even maintenance staff in company-logoed shirts move through the corridors he cleans each morning. He has developed a habit of tracking their locations on the floor before he begins a room, and he will delay entering a hallway if he knows one of them is at the far end. Colleagues have noticed that he is difficult to approach from behind; on two occasions, a coworker touched his shoulder to get his attention and Mateo spun around with a force that frightened them both. He has since been moved to a solo shift, which management framed as an accommodation but which has quietly reduced his hours and his contact with the rest of the team.

At night, Mateo rarely sleeps more than a few hours without waking. He will sit up in the dark, listening, sometimes moving to check that his front door is locked, sometimes simply remaining still until he is satisfied — by what, exactly, he cannot always say — that nothing is wrong. Strangers who approach him on the street, even to ask directions, produce a tightening across his chest and a rapid assessment of exits. He has come to believe that his body has simply recalibrated to a world where danger is everywhere and ordinary, and he is not entirely sure this belief is wrong.

Among the more disorienting aspects of his experience is what happens when something good occurs — a moment of laughter with a neighbor, a small pleasure at work, a feeling of warmth. These moments arrive and are almost immediately followed by a confusion that Mateo finds difficult to name, as though the feeling does not belong to him, or belongs to someone who no longer exists. He has stopped reaching for such moments. He smokes heavily, going through most of a pack a day, particularly in the evenings and during his breaks at work, when the cigarette gives his hands and attention somewhere to be.

His divorce was finalized six months ago. His former wife, whom he had married young and briefly, had found him impossible to reach. He does not dispute this. What finally brought Mateo to seek help was a letter from his employer noting that his performance had declined and that his isolation from the team had become a concern. He came not because he believed he could be helped, but because he was afraid of losing the only stable thing he has in this country. What he is most hoping for, he said quietly at the end of the intake, is to feel less like a stranger inside his own life.
